title: The Tale of Jemima Puddle-Duck
description: Published in 1908 and one of the most beloved of the tales: the story of a duck who wants to hatch her own eggs and is nearly eaten by a fox in a feathered hat. It is a prose fiction work of 1908 by Beatrix Potter; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale; Nonsense Verse and the Parody of Rule.
plot_or_argument: Jemima, whose eggs are always taken from her by the farmer's wife, is persuaded by a polite gentleman fox to lay them in his shed; the collie Kep rescues her and the eggs are eaten, but she hatches four ducklings at last.
narrative_structure: A story for children in short chapters, each of one sitting's length, the marvel named and repeated so that the child can follow it.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain. The author's characteristic manner is simple, concrete sentences.
historical_context: The 1900s, the Lake District farm, and the traditional English country lore of the fox and the duck. The record dates the work as composed between 1906 and 1908 and first published in 1908 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the dream-region tale; nonsense verse and the parody of rule.
literary_significance: Jemima Puddle-Duck is one of Potter's funniest and most deeply felt books, and one of the great English countryside stories for children; the fox's politeness is a permanent lesson in danger.

title: The Tale of Mr Tod
description: Published in 1912 and the darkest and most violent of the tales: the feud of the fox Mr Tod and the badger Mr Brock, and the kidnapping of the badger's son. It is a prose fiction work of 1912 by Beatrix Potter; it is catalogued here under Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale; Ghost Story and Scientific Supernatural Tale.
plot_or_argument: Mr Tod, the fox, keeps house with a family of rabbits and feuds with Mr Brock the badger; the badger's son is kidnapped, the rabbits dig a tunnel into the fox's kitchen, and the two animals destroy each other's houses in a long war.
narrative_structure: A story for children in short chapters, each of one sitting's length, the marvel named and repeated so that the child can follow it. A short narrative in which the witness's account is given first, the strange event is approached by stages, and the explanation is withheld at the close.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain. The author's characteristic manner is simple, concrete sentences.
historical_context: The 1910s, the Lake District woods and farms, and the natural history of the fox, the badger and the rabbit. The record dates the work as composed between 1909 and 1912 and first published in 1912 and it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the dream-region tale; ghost story and scientific supernatural tale.
literary_significance: Mr Tod is the most complex of Potter's books and the one in which her natural history becomes a study of the violence of the wild; it is a key text for the adult reading of Potter and for the environmental reading of children's literature.

title: Plain Tales from the Hills
description: Published in Calcutta in 1888 and Kipling's first collection of prose: forty short stories of Anglo-Indian life, written for the Civil and Military Gazette and the Pioneer, which made him famous at twenty-two.
plot_or_argument: The stories move through the stations and hill towns of British India — Simla, Lahore, Dalhousie — and record the marriages, adulteries, careers and disasters of the English, told in a hard, laconic voice and with an unerring sense of the small incident that reveals a life.
narrative_structure: A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
principal_characters: Mrs Hauksbee; Strickland of the Police; Mulvaney, Ortheris and Learoyd; Trejago and Bisesa ('Beyond the Pale'); Wressley of the Foreign Office; McIntosh Jellaludin ('To Be Filed for Reference'); Lispeth
literary_form: Collection of forty stories; local-colour sketch
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is terse, concrete narrative.
historical_context: The 1880s, the British Raj, the Simla season, the Indian Civil Service and the garrison, and the Anglo-Indian press. The record dates the work as composed between 1886 and 1888 and first published in 1888 and the corpus places it within Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire, it is catalogued under local-colour sketch and the regional portrait; realist novel of common life.
literary_significance: Plain Tales from the Hills invented the modern short story of colonial life and made Kipling the prose writer of the age at twenty-two: it gave English fiction a new subject, a new economy of style and a new voice, and it is the founding book of the literature of the British Raj.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Rudyard Kipling. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

title: The Jungle Book
description: Published in 1894 and one of the most influential books in the world: the stories of Mowgli, the boy raised by the wolves of the Seeonee hills, together with the animal tales of the white seal, Rikki-Tikki-Tavi and the elephants' dance.
plot_or_argument: Mowgli is adopted by Mother and Father Wolf and taught the Law of the Jungle by Baloo the bear and Bagheera the panther; he is hunted by Shere Khan the tiger, taken by the Bandar-log, and finally returns to the man-village, while the other stories follow the white seal's search for a safe island and the mongoose's war on the cobras.
narrative_structure: A story for children in short chapters, each of one sitting's length, the marvel named and repeated so that the child can follow it. A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery.
principal_characters: Mowgli; Father Wolf and Mother Wolf (Raksha); Akela; Baloo; Bagheera; Shere Khan; Tabaqui; Kaa; the Bandar-log; Messua; Kotick, the White Seal; Rikki-Tikki-Tavi; Nag and Nagaina; Little Toomai and Kala Nag
literary_form: Collection of animal stories and poems
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is terse, concrete narrative.
historical_context: The 1890s, the forests of the Central Provinces, the lore of the Indian jungle, and the Victorian animal story after Black Beauty. The record dates the work as composed between 1892 and 1894 and first published in 1894 and the corpus places it within Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire; Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the dream-region tale; imperial adventure romance.
literary_significance: The Jungle Book is the greatest English animal story of the century and one of the most influential books of the modern imagination: its Law of the Jungle, its Mowgli and its animal characters shaped the twentieth century's idea of nature and of childhood, and it is read as a parable of empire and of the feral child.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Rudyard Kipling. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Macmillan in London and New York in May 1894. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Barrack-Room Ballads
description: Published in 1892 and the volume that changed English poetry: ballads in the voice of the ordinary British soldier in India, sung in dialect and slang, with a rhythm learned from the music hall. It is a verse work of 1892 by Rudyard Kipling; it belongs to Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire and it is catalogued here under Dialect Poem and Vernacular Performance; War Narrative of the Common Soldier and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: 'Danny Deever' opens with the hanging of a soldier; 'Tommy' defends the private against the civilian's contempt; 'For to Admire' and 'Mandalay' celebrate and regret the East; 'Gunga Din' honours the native water-carrier; 'The Widow at Windsor' and 'Screw-Guns' record the soldier's view of the imperial machine.
narrative_structure: A collection of poems written to be performed, each a separate monologue or song in the spoken dialect.
meter_and_prosody: Ballad stanzas and music-hall metres, with heavy anaphora and refrain; mimetic dialect and soldiers' slang.
historical_context: The 1880s-90s, the British army in India and Egypt, the music hall and the new popular press, and the imperial jingoism of the Jubilee years. The record dates the work as composed between 1890 and 1892 and first published in 1892 and the corpus places it within Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire, it is catalogued under dialect poem and vernacular performance; war narrative of the common soldier.
literary_significance: Barrack-Room Ballads broke the Victorian poetic diction and made the private soldier a subject of lyric poetry; its influence on the language of popular verse, on Hardy, on the First World War poets and on the modern ballad is incalculable, and it remains the central poetic document of the British Empire.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Rudyard Kipling. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1892, as poetry collection, by Rudyard Kipling. Composed between 1890 and 1892. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Kim
description: Published in 1901 and the finest English novel of India: the story of Kimball O'Hara, an Irish orphan in Lahore, and of his wanderings with a Tibetan lama and his education as a spy in the Great Game.
plot_or_argument: Kim, the orphaned son of an Irish soldier, meets a Tibetan lama on a pilgrimage and becomes his chela; he is taken up by the British intelligence service, is educated at St Xavier's school, and travels the Grand Trunk Road gathering intelligence, until he finds the lama again and chooses the world.
narrative_structure: A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
principal_characters: Kimball O'Hara; the lama; Mahbub Ali; Colonel Creighton; Lurgan Sahib; Hurree Chunder Mookerjee; the Woman of Shamlegh; Teshoo Lama; the old soldier
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The author's characteristic manner is terse, concrete narrative.
historical_context: The 1880s-90s, the British Raj, the Indian railways and the Grand Trunk Road, the Great Game with Russia in Central Asia, and the lama's Buddhism. The record dates the work as composed between 1899 and 1901 and first published in 1901 and the corpus places it within Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire, it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance; novel of development and the growth story.
literary_significance: Kim is the finest English novel of India and one of the great novels of the twentieth century: its picture of the road, its double education of the boy and the lama, and its fusion of imperial intelligence work with Buddhist pilgrimage make it the central English text on the relation of East and West.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Rudyard Kipling. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Serialised in McClure's Magazine and Cassell's Magazine from December 1900 to October 1901 and published by Macmillan in London and by Doubleday, Page in New York in October 1901. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Just So Stories for Little Children
description: Published in 1902 and Kipling's book for his own children: twelve 'just so' stories of how the animals acquired their distinguishing features, told as comic fables of the earliest world. It is a prose fiction work of 1902 by Rudyard Kipling; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale; Nonsense Verse and the Parody of Rule and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: The collection gives the whale his throat, the camel his hump, the rhinoceros his skin, the leopard his spots, the elephant his trunk, the kangaroo his legs and the alphabet its letters, and ends with 'The Butterfly That Stamped'.
narrative_structure: A story for children in short chapters, each of one sitting's length, the marvel named and repeated so that the child can follow it.
principal_characters: the Whale and the Mariner; the Camel and the Djinn; the Parsee and the Rhinoceros; the Leopard and the Ethiopian; the Elephant's Child; Old Man Kangaroo; Taffy and Tegumai; the Cat that Walked by Himself; Suleiman-bin-Daoud and Balkis
literary_form: Collection of twelve tales (with the author's own illustrations)
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The text was issued with illustrations, which carry part of the meaning. The author's characteristic manner is terse, concrete narrative.
historical_context: The 1890s, the Victorian and Edwardian nursery, the evolutionary fable, and the Brer Rabbit tradition of the animal tale. The record dates the work as composed between 1897 and 1902 and first published in 1902 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade; Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire, it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the dream-region tale; nonsense verse and the parody of rule.
literary_significance: Just So Stories is one of the most inventive and beloved books in English and the finest comic prose Kipling wrote for children: its invented language, its nonsense logic and its invented cosmogonies made it a permanent nursery classic.

bibliographical_notes: First published in 1902, by Rudyard Kipling. Composed between 1897 and 1902. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Stalky & Co.
description: Published in 1899 and the most famous English school story after Tom Brown's Schooldays: the adventures of three boys at a second-rate public school and their war against the masters. It is a prose fiction work of 1899 by Rudyard Kipling; it belongs to Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire and it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Stalky, M'Turk and Beetle outwit the masters, run their own newspaper, avenge themselves on the school bullies, and in the last story return as officers in India, where their military cunning has been formed by the school.
narrative_structure: A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult. A story for children in short chapters, each of one sitting's length, the marvel named and repeated so that the child can follow it.
principal_characters: Stalky (Arthur Corkran); M'Turk; Beetle; the Head; Mr King; Mr Prout; the Reverend John Gillett
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is terse, concrete narrative.
historical_context: The 1870s, the United Services College at Westward Ho, the Victorian public school, and the imperial officer class. The record dates the work as composed between 1897 and 1899 and first published in 1899 and the corpus places it within Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire, it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; children's fantasy and the dream-region tale.
literary_significance: Stalky & Co. is the classic English public-school story and the central literary document of the education of the imperial elite; its amoral comedy and its celebration of loyalty and cunning made it the model for the modern school story and a key text in the history of English education.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Rudyard Kipling. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1899, as collection of school stories, by Rudyard Kipling. Composed between 1897 and 1899. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: The Story of an African Farm
description: Published in 1883 under the name Ralph Iron and the first great novel of the South African interior: the childhood and youth of three children on a Karoo farm, and the philosophical argument that is carried inside their story.
plot_or_argument: Waldo, the Boer-woman's son, Em, her daughter, and Lyndall, the orphaned English child, grow up on a sheep farm in the Karoo; the stranger Bonaparte Blenkins cheats the old Dutchwoman Tant' Sannie, the English overseer and the children's lives are shaped by the arrival of the stranger who calls himself the devil, and Lyndall goes away to school, is betrayed by a lover, and dies in a hotel room in Bloemfontein.
narrative_structure: A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
principal_characters: Lyndall; Em; Waldo; Tant' Sannie; Bonaparte Blenkins; Gregory Rose; the Stranger; Otto
literary_form: Novel (published under the pseudonym Ralph Iron, 1883)
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The author's characteristic manner is landscape description of the Karoo that is both exact and visionary.
historical_context: The 1860s-70s, the Karoo, the Boer farm economy, the English immigrants in the Cape, and the Victorian debate on evolution and faith. The record dates the work as composed between 1874 and 1881 and first published in 1883 and it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; realist novel of common life.
literary_significance: The Story of an African Farm is the founding novel of South African literature and one of the great English novels of the nineteenth century: it is the first novel to make the South African landscape a spiritual place, its heroine Lyndall is one of the earliest feminists in fiction, and its allegorical 'dream' chapters are among the most original things in Victorian prose.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Olive Emilie Albertina Schreiner. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published in three volumes by Chapman and Hall in London in January 1883 under the pseudonym Ralph Iron. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Woman and Labour
description: Published in 1911 and the most systematic work of feminist theory by a nineteenth-century English writer: a history and analysis of women's labour, and an argument for women's economic independence. It is a prose work of 1911 by Olive Schreiner; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: Schreiner argues that women have been historically the producers of the means of subsistence, that the industrial revolution destroyed their economic function, and that the claim for the vote and for work is a demand for the restoration of an ancient position rather than for a new privilege.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is landscape description of the Karoo that is both exact and visionary.
historical_context: The 1900s, the suffrage campaign, the new women's work of the 1890s, and the debate on the 'parasitic woman' that followed Lester Ward and Thorstein Veblen. The record dates the work as composed between 1897 and 1911 and first published in 1911 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; social inquiry and the documented survey.
literary_significance: Woman and Labour is a founding text of English feminist theory and the most important work of its kind between Wollstonecraft and Woolf: its argument about the economic function of women shaped the suffrage campaign and the twentieth-century analysis of women's work.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Olive Emilie Albertina Schreiner. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by T. Fisher Unwin in London in July 1911, having been written over twenty years. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Dreams
description: Published in 1890 and the finest of Schreiner's allegories: a series of dream-visions on hunters, strangers, women and death, written in a plain prose that has the quality of the Old Testament. It is a verse work of 1890 by Olive Schreiner; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Fable and Apologue.
plot_or_argument: In 'The Hunter' a man glimpses the reflection of the white bird of Truth, leaves the valley of superstition to seek her, and spends his life cutting steps into the mountains, dying with a single silver feather in his hand; in 'Three Dreams in a Desert' the history of women is unfolded in images of a woman bound to the earth beside a sleeping man, and of a woman who crosses the river of suffering towards the Land of Freedom on a track worn by the feet of those who went before.
narrative_structure: A collection of separate poems rather than a continuous narrative; the pieces stand alone and are commonly read individually.
principal_characters: the Hunter and the bird of Truth ('The Hunter'); the woman and Reason ('Three Dreams in a Desert')
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse: the line and stanza follow the conventions of the genre, and the poem is written to be read aloud. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is landscape description of the Karoo that is both exact and visionary.
historical_context: The 1890s, the vogue for the prose poem, the English reception of the Symbolists, and the allegorical tradition of Bunyan. The record dates the work as composed between 1888 and 1890 and first published in 1890 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under fable and apologue.
literary_significance: Dreams is the finest body of English allegory after Bunyan and the most original work of the 1890s: its prose poems were read as scripture by the feminist movement, and they anticipate the dream-visions of the modern short story.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Olive Emilie Albertina Schreiner. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by T. Fisher Unwin in London in March 1890. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Trooper Peter Halket of Mashonaland
description: Published in 1897 and the most direct English protest against the imperial conquest of southern Africa: the story of a trooper of the Chartered Company alone in the veld, and the stranger who comes to him.
plot_or_argument: Peter Halket, a trooper in Rhodes's Mashonaland, sits by his fire in the veld and is joined by a stranger who shows him the reality of what he has done in the name of empire, and of the hanging of a native chief; the trooper's conscience is awakened and the story ends with his death.
narrative_structure: A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery.
principal_characters: Peter Halket; the stranger; the captive Mashona man; the Captain
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The author's characteristic manner is landscape description of the Karoo that is both exact and visionary.
historical_context: The 1896-97, the Jameson Raid, the Matabele and Mashona risings, and the English debate on the Chartered Company's conduct. The record dates the work as composed between 1896 and 1897 and first published in 1897 and the corpus places it within Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire, it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance.
literary_significance: Trooper Peter Halket is the most important English literary protest against imperialism in the 1890s and a founding text of the anti-colonial novel: it was suppressed by the circulating libraries and it marks the beginning of the literary critique of empire from within English writing.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Olive Emilie Albertina Schreiner. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by T. Fisher Unwin in London in August 1897. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: While the Billy Boils
description: Published in 1896 and the founding book of Australian literature: sixty-two short pieces, most of them written in or after the year Lawson spent in the drought country around Bourke. It is a prose fiction work of 1896 by Henry Lawson; it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; Tall Tale and South-Western Humour Sketch and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: The stories give the bush in brief, hard anecdotes: the swagman and the squatter, the shearer and the cook, the mother and the lost child, the man who dies of thirst in the tank, the union men and the non-union men on the track.
narrative_structure: A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly. A framed sketch: the literate narrator, the vernacular teller, the escalating impossibility delivered deadpan and the punch that turns on the outsider.
principal_characters: the drover's wife; the bush undertaker; Mitchell, the swagman; Steelman; Arvie Aspinall
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is terse, laconic, anecdotal prose.
historical_context: The 1890s, the Australian shearers' strikes, the drought of 1891-95, the Bulletin school, and the federation movement. The record dates the work as composed between 1892 and 1896 and first published in 1896 and it is catalogued under local-colour sketch and the regional portrait; tall tale and south-western humour sketch.
literary_significance: While the Billy Boils created the Australian short story and made the bush the national place: its plain speech, its laconic narrator and its refusal of sentiment shaped Australian literature for the next century, and it is the first book in which Australian English is written as it is spoken.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Henry Archibald Hertzberg Lawson. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1896, as collection of stories and sketches, by Henry Lawson. Composed between 1892 and 1896. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: 'The Drover's Wife'
description: Published in the Bulletin in 1892 and the most famous Australian short story: a night in the life of a drover's wife alone on a selection with her children, while a snake hides under the house. It is a prose fiction work of 1892 by Henry Lawson; it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; Realist Novel of Common Life and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: The woman keeps watch through the night with her baby and her children and the dog Alligator, barricades the room, feeds the fire, thinks of her past and of her husband away with the cattle, and kills the snake with the dog's help.
narrative_structure: A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
principal_characters: the drover's wife; Tommy, her eldest son; Alligator, the dog; the snake; the absent drover, her husband
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The author's characteristic manner is terse, laconic, anecdotal prose.
historical_context: The 1890s, the woman on the selection, the absence of the drover, and the isolation of the Australian interior. The record dates the work as composed in 1892 and first published in 1892 and it is catalogued under local-colour sketch and the regional portrait; realist novel of common life.

title: Ancient Ballads and Legends of Hindustan
description: Published posthumously in 1882 and the first English retelling of the Indian epics by an Indian writer: ballads drawn from the Mahabharata, the Ramayana and the Puranas. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
